patch.value: password_assignment treats any value starting with a ${...} or $(...) reference as a placeholder, so a literal concatenated with a reference passes the guard

Reported 2026-11-10 by the fleet session from pm-memory#51's latest review (also commented on GH-1699). The flat value grammar in src/core/shared/secret-rules.ts (PASSWORD_VALUE) excludes every value whose first characters are '<', '${' or '$(' via a negative lookahead. A credential written as a literal next to an environment reference is therefore never judged: password=${EMPTY}"<literal>", password=$VAR"<literal>" and password=<literal>${VAR} pass both the SDK mutation guard and the repository scan. When the reference expands to nothing, the literal is the credential. A bare reference (password=${BUILD_PASSWORD}) must stay allowed, so a value is a placeholder only when the reference is the whole value. The structured pass added by pm-gh1699 inherits the same grammar, so quoted-key spellings behave the same way. This changes the flat rule, which also feeds the repository scan, so the change needs a repository-wide false-positive check like pm-gh1699's. Duplicate check: searched 'password placeholder reference concatenated literal env'. The pm-gh1699 must-allow corpus only covers whole-value references.

Must refuse in both consumers: a literal after a ${...} reference, after a $VAR reference, and before a ${...} reference, in flat and quoted-key spellings; Must allow in both consumers: a bare ${BUILD_PASSWORD}, a bare $(op read pw), a bare <placeholder> and an empty fallback; node scripts/check-secrets.mjs stays clean over every tracked file and the linear-time control still passes

A literal concatenated with an environment or command reference is judged as a credential, while a value that is only a reference stays allowed, in both the flat and structured spellings and in both consumers.
